# Laws, Paradoxes, and Fallacies of AI-Native Design {#sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes}

While the design principles throughout this book are its own (introduced in chapter design-principle callouts), the twelve phenomena collected here are borrowed. They include classical laws, statistical effects, and sociotechnical failure mechanisms, alongside architectural analogies that apply those ideas to learned components, generated candidates, and proxy surrogates inside a chip-design workflow. Most appear in chapter `Law` callouts at the point where the argument meets them; Simpson's paradox is included here as well to distinguish a statistical aggregation effect from the physical integration costs discussed in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack. This appendix serves as a companion reference, bringing all twelve phenomena together with their classical origins, the forms they can take in architecture work, and their countermeasures (@tbl-laws-paradoxes-summary).

Four of the twelve phenomena require a derivation or quantitative model that would interrupt a chapter callout: the optimizer's curse, the winner's curse, the Jevons paradox, and queueing congestion collapse. Those four receive full entries below, while the remaining eight receive shorter entries that state the phenomenon, name the failure mode it helps identify in architecture work, and point to the relevant chapter discussion where applicable. Whenever an entry uses a constructed scenario to illustrate a mechanism, the text labels that scenario as constructed; any numbers in such an illustration are hypothetical rather than measured.

| **Phenomenon and classical origin** | **Mechanism or conditional bound** | **Form it takes in AI-for-hardware work** | **Countermeasure and related discussion** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **1. Goodhart's Law** [@Goodhart1984Monetary; @Strathern1997Goodhart] | Optimization pressure can weaken the relationship between a target metric and the quality it is intended to measure. | An optimizer may insert unjustified `set_false_path` constraints or remove required reset logic that the checks fail to test. | Evaluator-owned constraints and blind-spot red-teaming (@sec-law-goodhart; @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect). |
| **2. The Optimizer's Curse** [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse] | Selecting the largest of individually unbiased estimates can make the selected estimate optimistic. | Surrogate-driven search can select extreme configurations where positive proxy error is large. | Screening audits under the actual selection procedure and independent confirmation matched to the claim (@sec-law-optimizers-curse; @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). |
| **3. The Winner's Curse** [@CapenEtAl1971CompetitiveBidding; @Thaler1988WinnersCurse] | Winning with an unadjusted valuation can select optimistic error; candidate optimization sweeps exhibit a related selection effect. | A top-ranked candidate may benefit from sampling variation or a simulator artifact rather than repeatable power, performance, and area (PPA) gains. | Confirmatory reruns on held-out seeds and disjoint workload kernels (@sec-law-winners-curse; @sec-feedback-verification-trust). |
| **4. The Streetlight Effect** [@Kaplan1964ConductOfInquiry] | Search concentrates where measurement is easy rather than where the defects are. | An evaluation confined to single-clock leaf modules leaves multi-clock system-on-chip (SoC) interfaces untested. | Complexity audits and SoC-scale benchmark suites (@sec-law-streetlight-effect; @sec-data-representations-world-models). |
| **5. Ironies of Automation** [@Bainbridge1983Ironies] | Automation can reduce routine diagnostic practice while leaving operators responsible for faults outside its capabilities. | Engineers who rarely inspect tool results may lack practice diagnosing layout or protocol failures. | Diagnostic failure laboratories and fault-injection training (@sec-law-ironies-automation; @sec-curriculum-certification). |
| **6. Moral Crumple Zones** [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones] | Responsibility can be misattributed to a human who had little control over an automated system. | A signing engineer may bear blame for a generated block without having had meaningful control over its review. | Meaningful review access, decision authority, and organizational responsibility (@sec-law-moral-crumple-zones; @sec-what-architect-owns). |
| **7. Normalization of Deviance** [@Vaughan1996Challenger] | Repeated acceptance of anomalies can normalize risk when the absence of failure substitutes for justification. | Unresolved clock-domain-crossing (CDC) warnings or design-rule violations are waived because a loop could not close the proof. | Justified, traceable waivers with named owners and reconsideration criteria (@sec-law-normalization-deviance; @sec-what-architect-owns). |
| **8. The Jevons Paradox** [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion] | Total resource use can rise when growth in activity outweighs reduced use per activity; see the entry's conditional model. | Cheaper register-transfer level (RTL) generation can increase candidate arrivals to expensive verification tools. | Admission control, multi-fidelity filtering, queue stability (@sec-law-jevons-paradox; @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales). |
| **9. Amdahl's Law for Teams** [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor] | $S = \frac{1}{(1-f) + f/s}$ for fixed, additive work with no added overhead; $(1-f)$ is the unchanged fraction. | Drafting acceleration has limited schedule impact when drafting is a small share of sequential elapsed time. | Identify unchanged work and critical-path limits (@sec-law-amdahls-law-teams; @sec-moonshot). |

Simpson's Paradox** [@Simpson1951ContingencyTables] | A trend present in every subgroup can reverse when the subgroups are aggregated with different weights. | Aggregate comparisons can reverse subgroup comparisons when the evaluated workload mixtures differ. | Inspect subgroup results and aggregation weights; distinguish this statistical effect from integration overhead (@sec-law-simpsons-paradox). |

: **Twelve borrowed laws, paradoxes, and fallacies recur across AI-native computer architecture.** Each row pairs a classical principle from economics, statistics, queueing theory, or human factors with the form it takes in hardware workflows and its corresponding countermeasure. {#tbl-laws-paradoxes-summary tbl-colwidths="[18,24,30,28]"}

The sections that follow expand each row of @tbl-laws-paradoxes-summary. For the optimizer's curse and the winner's curse, the algebra shows why selecting the top estimate introduces upward bias; for the Jevons paradox, the model shows how falling unit cost can raise total tool demand; and for congestion collapse, the queueing approximation links turnaround delay to the share of results that return after a design question has moved on. The shorter entries around them provide quick reference and clarify boundaries such as the difference between statistical aggregation in Simpson's paradox and unmodeled physical coupling during system integration.

## Goodhart's Law and Constraint Tampering {#sec-law-goodhart}

When a measure becomes a target, it can lose its usefulness as a measure [@Strathern1997Goodhart; @Goodhart1984Monetary]. In architecture work, an optimizer that is allowed to modify the files that grade it may improve its reported score without improving the hardware, for instance by inserting an unjustified `set_false_path` into a timing constraint file or deleting an assertion from a testbench. A related failure occurs inside the design itself when an optimizer strips out required reset logic from a netlist and an incomplete test suite rewards the resulting area or timing reduction despite the lost behavior.

When the evaluation harness locks timing constraints and testbenches under independent evaluator control, the design optimizer can no longer weaken those checks directly, though locking the files still does not establish that the test suite covers every functional requirement. Red-teaming the loop for constraint and testbench tampering before admitting a result can help verify that this separation holds in practice, as @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect develops in detail.

## The Optimizer's Curse in Proxy Search {#sec-law-optimizers-curse}

**The classical principle.** Smith and Winkler showed that selecting the alternative with the highest estimated value from a set of noisy estimates can yield an upwardly biased estimate of the selected alternative's true value [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. Let true values be $v_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma_v^2)$ and proxy estimates be $\hat{v}_i = v_i + \epsilon_i$ with estimation error $\epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\epsilon^2)$. Assume the true values and errors are independent across candidates and that the errors are independent of the true values. For the selected candidate $i^* = \arg\max_{i=1..N} \hat{v}_i$, the expected true value conditional on the observed estimate $\hat{y}$ is
$$\mathbb{E}[v_{i^*} \mid \hat{v}_{i^*} = \hat{y}] = \mu + \frac{\sigma_v^2}{\sigma_v^2 + \sigma_\epsilon^2}(\hat{y} - \mu).$$
For an observed maximum $\hat{y} > \mu$ and nonzero estimation variance, this conditional expectation falls below $\hat{y}$, yielding a conditional post-decision disappointment of $\Delta_{\text{curse}} = \hat{y} - \mathbb{E}[v_{i^*} \mid \hat{y}] = \frac{\sigma_\epsilon^2}{\sigma_v^2 + \sigma_\epsilon^2}(\hat{y} - \mu)$ that increases with estimation variance when the observation and prior variance are held fixed. Although that conditional expression for a fixed $\hat{y}$ contains no pool-size term, pool size enters across repeated draws because searching a larger pool tends to produce a higher selected estimate. For independent candidates under this Gaussian model, the expected sample maximum scales for large $N$ as $\mathbb{E}[\max_{i=1..N} \hat{v}_i] \approx \mu + \sqrt{\sigma_v^2 + \sigma_\epsilon^2}\sqrt{2\ln N}$, so expected disappointment grows with $N$ when the variances are held fixed.

**The form it takes in architecture work.** During design-space exploration, teams often train learned surrogates (Gaussian processes, gradient-boosted trees, or neural networks) on sparse simulation traces so that candidates can be scored quickly. When a search algorithm selects candidates along the surrogate's predicted upper frontier, it can favor positive approximation errors alongside genuinely high values. Sparsely trained regions of the design space may be especially vulnerable, even though errors from a shared surrogate need not follow the independent Gaussian model above. In a constructed out-of-order core exploration, for example, an uncalibrated surrogate selects an extreme reorder-buffer depth paired with a very wide issue window because it predicts record instructions per cycle; that performance estimate does not establish that the circuit can meet its target clock, and in this constructed case unmodeled bypass-network delay causes the netlist to fail static timing analysis.

**The countermeasure.** An evaluation harness should preserve the predictions made before selection and compare finalists against independent reference-tool returns (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). Prediction intervals and ranking audits can help diagnose screening error, but their behavior must be checked under the actual selection procedure because calibration on ordinary candidates does not establish reliability at the search frontier. When candidates leave the training distribution's declared support, surrogate screening should be suspended. Final confirmation then matches the scope of the claim: a simulator-level ranking requires reference simulation under declared conditions, whereas a physical timing claim requires timing evidence. Neither an uncertainty estimate nor a favorable proxy rank replaces that check.

## The Winner's Curse in Candidate Optimization Sweeps {#sec-law-winners-curse}

**The classical principle.** Capen, Clapp, and Campbell identified the winner's curse in offshore oil-tract auctions [@CapenEtAl1971CompetitiveBidding], and Thaler reviewed experimental and field evidence for it [@Thaler1988WinnersCurse]. In a common-value auction, bidders estimate the value of the same underlying asset from incomplete information; when bids follow those unadjusted estimates without accounting for selection, winning can favor the bidder with the most optimistic estimation error.

**The form it takes in architecture work.** In an optimization sweep, a search method may propose dozens of competing microarchitectural variants (cache replacement policies, prefetcher triggers, network-on-chip arbiters) that are graded on randomized simulation seeds or truncated benchmark windows. Because these variants have different underlying performance, the common-value auction serves as an analogy, yet picking the highest measured score can still favor a variant whose run benefited from sampling variation rather than one whose advantage persists across runs. An uninitialized warm-up trace or a fixed-latency simulator artifact can also create an apparent advantage, though those represent evaluation defects or modeling limitations rather than simple sampling luck. This selection mechanism overlaps with the optimizer's curse (@sec-law-optimizers-curse) because optimistic errors can be selected whether they arise in a learned surrogate or in a simulation-based evaluation, and higher model fidelity alone does not eliminate finite-sample variation. For a fixed finite set of candidates, let $v_i$ be each candidate's true value, with higher values preferred, and let $\hat{v}_i$ be an unbiased estimate of that value. Selecting $I = \arg\max_i \hat{v}_i$ gives
$$\mathbb{E}[\hat{v}_I-v_I] \ge 0.$$
Here the expectation is taken over repeated evaluations of the candidate set [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. Because the expected maximum estimate is at least the largest true value while the selected candidate's expected true value cannot exceed that largest value, the winning estimate is optimistic on average.

**The countermeasure.** Before accepting a winning candidate, the architect needs independent confirmatory evaluation matched to the claim (@sec-feedback-verification-trust). In practice, confirmation entails rerunning the top-ranked variant and its comparison baseline on held-out random seeds, checking sensitivity to truncated windows through full-program simulation or a suitable sampling approach such as SimPoint or SMARTS (without describing sampled execution as full-program execution), and evaluating disjoint workload kernels when the claim extends to unseen workloads. Because repeated runs on new seeds can still preserve the same warm-up artifact or simulator assumption, those modeling conditions must be checked separately before accepting the improvement to the extent supported by the evidence.

## The Streetlight Effect in Hardware AI Benchmarks {#sec-law-streetlight-effect}

In Kaplan's parable, a drunkard searches for his lost keys under a streetlight because the light is better there, not because the keys fell there [@Kaplan1964ConductOfInquiry]. Benchmark design can fall into a similar pattern when evaluation concentrates on what is cheap to grade, such as shallow, single-clock Verilog leaf modules paired with Python testbenches. Concentrating there leaves defects at multi-clock system-on-chip interfaces, credit-based interconnects, and reset-sequencing state machines untested, so a generator that scores well under the streetlight remains blind to those system-level failure modes. The corpus comparison in @sec-data-representations-world-models measures the resulting structural differences between sampled benchmark modules and sampled production-oriented register-transfer level (RTL) code, and its `Law` callout explains why claims about deeper hierarchy or multi-clock behavior require evaluations that exercise those structures.

## Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation in Hardware Design {#sec-law-ironies-automation}

Bainbridge described a central irony of automated systems: automating routine tasks can reduce an operator's everyday opportunity to practice, even as the human remains responsible for handling unanticipated faults beyond the automation's capabilities [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. In hardware design, engineers who prompt a generator but rarely inspect a waveform, a clock-tree skew report, or a placement density map may have fewer opportunities to build the diagnostic skills needed when a design loop cannot resolve an intermittent protocol deadlock or a voltage droop. Dedicated failure laboratories can preserve regular practice in reading tool evidence and isolating faults alongside training in prompting. @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem discusses diagnostic fault-injection training in its `Law` callout, and @sec-what-architect-owns applies this irony to the architect's signoff role.

## Moral Crumple Zones and Nondelegable Signoff {#sec-law-moral-crumple-zones}

Elish coined the term *moral crumple zone* for the misattribution of responsibility to a human operator who had limited control over an automated system [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. In chip design, the analogy highlights what can go wrong when review consists of signing a dashboard summary of thousands of automated runs: the signing engineer may bear the blame for a tapeout failure despite having had little opportunity to examine or influence the design choices that produced it.

An inspectable evidence package and an explicit statement of residual risk can support signoff, but naming a human signer does not by itself settle the allocation of responsibility. The reviewing engineer also needs schedule time to inspect the evidence and institutional authority to request further checks or refuse commitment. Nondelegable signoff should protect that engineer's judgment without making an individual solely responsible for failures shaped by the organization's tools, review practices, and resource decisions (@sec-what-architect-owns).

## Normalization of Deviance in Verification Waivers {#sec-law-normalization-deviance}

Vaughan's analysis of the *Challenger* loss describes how repeatedly accepted anomalies can become normal operating practice when an organization takes the absence of immediate failure as evidence of safety [@Vaughan1996Challenger]. In architecture work, an analogous drift arises when a design loop cannot close a formal proof or a timing check and the team begins accepting unresolved warnings because earlier designs appeared to work. An unconstrained clock-domain crossing or a design-rule violation may then receive a waiver based on precedent rather than on evidence that the exception is justified. Even when a block passes at a typical corner, that result does not establish that the waived condition is harmless across other operating conditions, where an escape could still force a respin.

Granting a waiver is not by itself evidence of deviance; the distinction lies in whether the technical justification remains reviewable or whether repeated acceptance quietly substitutes for analysis. Version-controlled waiver records with a named owner and an expiration point make exceptions traceable and identify when they require reconsideration, though the records alone do not establish that a waiver is sound (@sec-what-architect-owns).

## The Jevons Paradox of Automated Generation {#sec-law-jevons-paradox}

**The classical principle.** Jevons argued in *The Coal Question* that more efficient resource use can stimulate enough additional activity to increase total consumption [@Jevons1865CoalQuestion]. Let $c_{\text{unit}}$ denote resource use per activity, $D(c)$ the number of activities undertaken at that resource intensity, and $C_{\text{total}}$ total resource use. If resource use per activity falls, total use rises only when activity grows by more than the inverse of that reduction. Under this demand response, the mechanism is
$$c_{\text{unit}} \downarrow \implies D(c) \uparrow\uparrow \implies C_{\text{total}} = c_{\text{unit}} \cdot D(c) \uparrow.$$
If unit cost instead denotes money, the product measures expenditure and does not directly measure physical resource consumption.

**The form it takes in architecture work.** Consider a hypothetical generator that reduces the marginal effort of producing an RTL block or a floorplan candidate from weeks of engineering labor to seconds of inference, a comparison that illustrates cheaper candidate production rather than measuring compute savings. If the design loop responds by generating and submitting many more candidates, aggregate verification demand can rise even as drafting becomes cheaper. Every candidate admitted to later stages still requires gate-level simulation, static timing analysis, design-rule checking, or layout-versus-schematic verification matched to the artifact and decision, and faster RTL generation does not by itself make those downstream checks any cheaper. When the resulting tool demand exceeds available capacity, it can saturate compute clusters and exhaust commercial electronic design automation license pools. That conditional demand rebound forms the demand-side companion to @sec-law-congestion-collapse, where the queue model below describes what happens to the tool stage receiving the load.

**The countermeasure.** To prevent cheap generation from flooding downstream tools, a closed-loop system can place a multi-fidelity evaluation funnel and admission backpressure in front of its expensive stages (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization). Analytical rooflines and fast formal checks can filter out weak candidates before they reach signoff tools, though those early filters support screening only within their modeling assumptions and any candidate that advances still requires the checks appropriate to its stage. Admission to expensive evaluation should therefore be governed by available verification capacity rather than by the generator's proposing speed.

## Amdahl's Law for Semiconductor Teams {#sec-law-amdahls-law-teams}

Amdahl's law bounds speedup for a fixed amount of work when an improvement accelerates only part of the original execution time and adds no coordination overhead:
$$S = 1/((1-f) + f/s),$$
where $f$ is the fraction of the original execution time affected by the improvement and $s$ is its local speedup [@Amdahl1967ValiditySingleProcessor]. The unaffected fraction, $1-f$, limits the overall gain: as $s$ grows without bound, $S$ approaches $1/(1-f)$ for $f < 1$.

Applying this relationship to a chip-design schedule is an analogy that requires care. Across sequential stages with fixed work, if a tool accelerates RTL drafting while leaving verification, physical design, timing closure, and post-silicon validation unchanged, the same algebraic bound holds with $f$ measured as drafting's share of the original elapsed time. The whole-project gain can be substantial when that share is large, and small when drafting occupies little of the schedule. When project stages overlap in time, moreover, their durations cannot simply be added: reducing total elapsed time depends on shortening tasks along the critical path, and the critical path itself may shift after an improvement.

For the discussion in @sec-moonshot, the key question is which schedule bottlenecks a proposed tool or design loop can actually change. A system that also reduces verification or timing-closure effort may relax limits that faster RTL drafting leaves intact, but its schedule advantage must be established from the resulting critical path and work rather than inferred from Amdahl's law alone.

## Queueing Congestion Collapse in Tool Loops {#sec-law-congestion-collapse}

**The classical principle.** For an illustrative M/M/1 queue with Poisson arrivals at rate $\lambda$, exponentially distributed service times with rate $\mu$, and $\lambda < \mu$, the mean time a job spends waiting and in service is $W = \frac{1}{\mu - \lambda}$. Little's law, $L = \lambda W$, relates that turnaround time to the mean number of requests in the system, $L$ [@Kleinrock1975QueueingSystems; @Little1961LittlesLaw].

**The form it takes in architecture work.** When a generator in closed-loop exploration proposes candidates at rate $g$ and pushes a downstream tool stage to or past stability ($\rho_i = \lambda_i / \mu_i \ge 1$), an unbounded queue has no finite steady-state mean wait time. Even below capacity, queueing delay may allow a specification or interface contract to change before a tool run returns, which means the team must reconsider whether the returned result still applies to the active design question even though the log still describes the inputs that ran. To express this effect in a constructed approximation, suppose relevant specification changes follow a Poisson process independent of tool execution with positive rate $\gamma_{\text{drift}}$, define a fresh return as one with no such change during its age, and use mean turnaround $W$ as a representative age for each return. Here the scale $1/\gamma_{\text{drift}}$ is a characteristic change interval rather than a deterministic expiration time, and $W > 1/\gamma_{\text{drift}}$ does not by itself make recorded evidence invalid. Under those assumptions, the approximation models the rate of returns still applicable to the active question as
$$V_{\text{eff}}(\lambda) = \lambda \cdot P(\text{fresh}) = \lambda \cdot e^{-\gamma_{\text{drift}} W} = \lambda \cdot e^{-\frac{\gamma_{\text{drift}}}{\mu - \lambda}}.$$
As $\lambda \to \mu$ from below with $\gamma_{\text{drift}} > 0$, this model gives $W \to \infty$ and $V_{\text{eff}} \to 0$. That limit belongs to the stated mean-age approximation and is not a claim that older results cease to describe their recorded inputs or lose all later value; an exact calculation for a random queue would average freshness over the distribution of job ages rather than substituting the mean.

**The countermeasure.** Execution harnesses enforce a feed-forward stability bound on the generator, $g < \min_i (\mu_i / \prod p_j)$, where $p_j$ are the pass fractions of the upstream filters and each stage's product includes only the filters before that stage, with the first stage taking an empty product equal to one. This baseline bound assumes a feed-forward chain with one downstream job per surviving candidate and no retries or external arrivals; stages behind a zero upstream pass fraction receive no work and impose no bound, whereas branching workflows, repeated checks, and tool retries require their additional arrivals to be counted. The harness therefore combines that feed-forward estimate with live telemetry backpressure that throttles generation whenever a downstream queue approaches capacity, $\rho_i \to 1$ (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization; @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces).

## Simpson's Paradox and the Aggregation Boundary {#sec-law-simpsons-paradox}

Simpson showed that a trend present in every subgroup can disappear or reverse when the subgroups are aggregated with different weights [@Simpson1951ContingencyTables]. In an architecture comparison, that reversal can occur whenever two reported summary scores use different workload mixtures; inspecting the subgroup results alongside the aggregation weights reveals whether an aggregate ranking reflects a genuine hardware difference or a shift in what was measured.

The system-integration example in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack operates through a different mechanism. There, a candidate systolic array ties the baseline on simulated cycle count, but its dataflow folding doubles the modeled off-chip memory writes, a cost that the local cycle metric did not count. Because no reversal of subgroup statistics is needed when a local measurement simply omits costs that appear outside the block, catching that problem requires an enclosing measurement boundary that exposes the off-chip traffic. Distinguishing the two mechanisms tells the architect what to inspect: aggregation weights and workload mix for Simpson's paradox, versus omitted cross-boundary interactions for an integration failure.

## The Whac-a-Mole Regression Effect {#sec-law-whac-a-mole}

When an optimization loop targets a single metric, changes in other properties can go unobserved. A related lesson comes from distributed-systems recovery testing, where FATE and DESTINI pair systematic failure exploration with explicit checks for outcomes such as availability and data loss [@GunawiEtAl2011FATEDestini]. That analogy motivates checking every outcome that matters for signoff, not only the metric being optimized.

In a constructed timing-repair example, an optimizer may widen cell drivers and insert repeaters to close a local timing violation. While those edits improve slack on the target path, they can also increase local current demand and routing congestion, creating physical costs outside the timing objective whose severity depends on the implementation and operating conditions. The countermeasure developed in @sec-feedback-verification-trust is to track the full set of relevant quantities and check all functional and physical properties required for the scoped decision before accepting a repair, rather than treating an improved timing metric as sufficient evidence.
